about: T10 captions, written as a warm tutor speaking; each line starts at film time t (seconds). Can be recorded as voiceover later.

lines.text: Lesson ten: a tour of an exchange platform. Let's learn the screen, one piece at a time.
Open any trading app and you'll see a screen like this. So many boxes!
This is an educational mock, not a real exchange screen. Real apps look different and change often.
But they share the same few parts.
Think of it like a car dashboard. Each part has one job.
Watchlist, symbol bar and chart. Order book and order entry.
Positions at the bottom, and your wallet and security up top.
We'll visit each one. No real orders, no real money.
First, the watchlist. It's a list of trading pairs you want to keep an eye on.
Type BTC in the search box, and the list narrows to Bitcoin.
Tap BTC/USDT, and the whole screen switches to that pair.
Up top is the symbol bar. A symbol is the short name of a market, like BTCUSDT.
Next to it: the last traded price, and the change over the past 24 hours.
Example: 24 hours ago, 60,000. Now 61,200. That's up 1,200 USDT, or +2%.
The chart shows price over time. Each candle covers one slice of time, like one minute.
Watch the newest candle form. It grows as trades happen at new prices.
Tabs like 1m, 5m and 15m change the time slice. T14 and T15 cover this.
The order book lists waiting orders: sellers' asks on top, buyers' bids below.
The gap between the best ask and the best bid is the spread. Here: 60,010 − 60,000 = 10 USDT.
When a market buy arrives, it takes the best ask, and the last price ticks up.
The order entry panel is where an order is set up. Choose a type: limit, market or stop.
Enter a price and a size. Say a limit buy at 60,000 for 0.010 BTC.
Order value is price × size: 60,000 × 0.010 = 600 USDT. The fee estimate shows too.
Here the buttons are mock only. No real order is sent.
Once an order fills, it becomes a position, listed at the bottom of the screen.
PnL means profit and loss. Unrealized PnL is your result so far, on an open position.
Long 0.010 BTC from 60,000. Price 60,600: +6 USDT. Price 59,400: −6 USDT.
It's only realized when you close the position.
Your wallet shows the money in your account. Here, a fictional 1,000 USDT.
Part of it is in use, held for open orders and positions. The rest is available.
Example: 1,000 − 600 in use = 400 USDT available for new orders.
Last stop: security settings. They protect your account.
Two-factor login asks for a second code from your phone, as well as your password.
An anti-phishing code appears in real emails from the exchange, so fakes stand out.
API keys let software use your account. Never share them, or any code. XORA never asks.
A common mistake: learning where the buttons sit, instead of what they say.
Apps update. Here, an update swaps the buttons. A tap from memory hits Sell, not Buy.
Correction: always read the label, and check the order before you confirm.
Your turn. Where would you look to see your unrealized PnL? Pause if you need more time.
The answer is C, the positions panel. It shows your open positions and their PnL.
Not A, the chart. The chart shows the market price, not your own result.
First, some safety rules for real apps.
Check the address. A look-alike website can steal your login.
Check which market you're in, spot or futures, before any order.
Never tap around a real account to explore. A tap can place a real order.
And WAIT, or no trade, is always a valid choice.
Every trading screen is built from the same parts, each with one job.
Positions show your unrealized PnL. The wallet shows what's still available.
Read every label, protect your account, and never share keys or codes.
Check yourself: where do you find the spread?
In the order book: the gap between the best ask and the best bid.
Great work! Next up, T11: spot versus futures. What do you really own?
